newsitem.title: USA: U.S. says expects France to join Iraq air patrols.
newsitem.headline: U.S. says expects France to join Iraq air patrols.

text.p: The White House said on Wednesday it was confident that France soon would join the United States and Britain in a renewed operation barring Iraqi flights over northern Iraq.
Dismissing reports of a possible new rift with Paris, the White House said it expected France to sign on to the continued air patrols "within the next few days."

The new patrols are a follow-on to Operation Provide Comfort, whose mandate runs out on Dec. 31. The Turkish parliament voted on Wednesday to let the new patrols begin on Jan. 1 from a base in Turkey.
In Ankara, a Turkish Foreign Ministry official said France had made it known during talks on the new operation that it was not ready for an agreement on technical issues "at the moment."
"French authorities will study the new conditions created by this decision and will make their position known at the right time," a French foreign ministry spokesman said in Paris.
But David Johnson, a White House spokesman, said the United States fully expected "that within the next few days all of the 'i's will be dotted and the 't's will be crossed."

"The French were simply reluctant to go through something formal on Christmas Day -- to go through all the things that they needed to do in order to do that," he told Reuters in a telephone interview.
He said the United States was confident that "all three coalition partners would be enforcing the no-fly zone in northern Iraq, just as they have in the past.
"It will remain a no-fly zone, and if necessary they will take action against any hostile Iraqi aircraft that are north of the line," he added.

Separately, the State Department welcomed a vote in Turkey's parliament to extend coalition air operations over northern Iraq. "Coalition aircraft will continue to fly these operations, as they have since 1991," John Dinger, a department spokesman, said in a statement. He said the designation "Provide Comfort" would no longer be used.

"The ongoing air operation underscores the firm commitment of coalition partners to bringing about Iraq's full compliance" with the United Nations resolutions that ended the 1991 Gulf War, the State Department said.

Allied aircraft have been shielding Iraq's ethnics Kurds from Iraqi aircraft north of the 36th parallel since a failed Kurdish uprising at the end of the war. The operation has been based at Incerlik Air Base in Turkey.
The nature of any French objections was not immediately clear. A Western diplomatic source in Turkey said Paris might pull out entirely. "It seems like they won't participate," he said.

France and the United States have been at odds this month over the U.S. command of NATO forces in southern Europe, French objections to the appointment of U.N. Secretary-General-elect Kofi Annan and a perceived diplomatic snub of outgoing Secretary of State Warren Christopher.

France has supplied about half a dozen planes to the northern Iraq contingent of some 50 aircraft. It temporarily halted its flights in September after the United States fired 44 cruise missiles against targets in the south to punish President Saddam Hussein for moving Iraqi ground troops into a Kurdish enclave north of the 36th parallel.
Paris, eager to help exploit Iraqi oil resources, has courted Baghdad's favour and pressed for a conditional end to United Nations sanctions against Iraq.
